message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Food Waste Collection

The cost table adds up and the pilot data are genuinely useful. However, three central claims don't survive the document's own figures: that flats participated at similar rates, the 3,290-tonne projection, and "fully funded." On top of that, Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage. Cabinet would be approving a vehicle order on the strength of this paper, so these points need fixing first.

## 1. Flats did not participate at a similar rate to houses

Table 1 shows **66% participation for houses and 21% for flats**. Flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses, and also produced less food waste per participating household (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg).

The text, the recommendation and your summary all say participation was "broadly similar" and that a uniform service will work. The data point the other way. Flats are about 20% of the district, roughly 10,400 households, and the pilot suggests the standard caddy service largely fails for them. Low participation in flats is a well-known pattern, usually tackled with communal bins, bin-store access arrangements and targeted communications. The study should plan a separate approach for flats and cost it.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate that isn't in the pilot

Section 3 applies **"the pilot's 64% participation rate."** The pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and 64% appears nowhere in Table 1. The 3,290 tonnes is calculated from that figure.

The pilot's housing mix happens to match the district's (20% flats in both), so the pilot can be scaled up directly:

| Housing | District households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | about 2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | about 160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **about 2,870** |

That is about **13% below** the study's figure. Two smaller points:
- The "All" yield of 1.9 kg is rounded up. The weighted figure is 1.86 kg.
- Pilots tend to overstate long-term participation, because of novelty and extra attention during the pilot. The January to June period may also not represent a full year. A sensitivity range would be prudent.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the tonnage

Section 4 states that Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Both the study's 3,290 tonnes and the corrected 2,870 tonnes exceed this, by **about 1,100–1,500 tonnes a year**. The surplus would have to go to the next plant, **46 miles away**, at a gate fee that isn't stated and with significant extra haulage costs.

The study takes the £74/tonne saving across *all* the tonnage, as if all of it went to Brookfield. Your summary's statement that "treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away" is true for at most about 60% of the food waste.

This needs either a costed arrangement for the surplus, or confirmation that Brookfield's capacity can be increased before 2029.

## 4. "Fully funded" doesn't hold

**The cost table is correct.** Vehicles: £990,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400. Crews: £408,000. Total £733,400, and net £490,400 as stated.

**The disposal saving is overstated:**
- At the corrected 2,870 t, all treated at Brookfield, the saving is about **£212,000**. Net cost is about **£521,000**, roughly equal to the £520,000 allocation, with no headroom.
- With the Brookfield cap, and assuming haulage cancels out the saving on the roughly 1,070 t sent elsewhere, the saving is 1,800 × £74 = **£133,000**. Net cost is about **£600,000**, which is **about £80,000 above** the allocation.

**Costs the table leaves out**, all of which push the net cost further up:
- spare or cover vehicles (six vehicles for six rounds leaves no margin for breakdowns or servicing)
- cover for crew leave and sickness (12 operatives with no relief staff)
- supervision and management
- recruitment and training
- staffing the dedicated phone line and web page
- any financing cost on the vehicles
- haulage to the second plant
- a separate service for flats (see point 1)

Your summary says "every cost line is shown." The lines shown are correct, but they don't add up to the full cost of running the service.

**The funding isn't confirmed either.** The £520,000 is "provisional," and the Government has "indicated" it will provide funding. Cabinet should see what happens if the final allocation comes in lower.

## 5. Timetable and statutory deadline

- **Vehicle lead time.** Ordering in December for delivery in March allows about three months. Specialist food waste vehicles have often had considerably longer lead times. Confirm the date in writing with the supplier before relying on it. If delivery slips, the April start date slips with it.
- **The statutory deadline.** Under the Simpler Recycling reforms, English councils were generally required to start weekly food waste collections by **31 March 2026**, with transitional arrangements for some councils with existing contracts. A start date of April 2027 implies Thornbury either has such an arrangement or is already late. The study should say which, because it affects both the urgency and the risk of the decision.

## 6. Smaller points

- **The 81% satisfaction figure** is described only as from "surveyed pilot households." Give the sample size and response rate. People who use the service are more likely to answer a survey about it.
- **The low contamination figure** (under 2%) is a strength, though spot checks at the plant may not reflect the flats.
- **The implementation section has no risks.** Add vehicle delay, recruitment, and capacity at Brookfield.

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the "broadly similar" claim and add a costed plan for flats.
2. Use the pilot's actual rates by housing type to project about 2,870 t, and give a range.
3. Explain how the roughly 1,000+ tonnes above Brookfield's 1,800 t cap will be handled and what it will cost.
4. Rebuild the net cost with the capacity limit, cover vehicles and staff, supervision and the other missing items. Compare it with the allocation under a low-funding scenario.
5. Confirm the vehicle lead time and the Council's position on the statutory deadline.
6. Change "fully funded" to whatever the corrected figures support.

The service may still be the right decision, and it is likely a statutory requirement anyway. But as written, the study overstates participation, tonnage and savings, and understates costs. Cabinet should approve the roll-out on corrected figures.
